issues.legal_issue: A gift of land made without consideration is not a transfer for consideration within the statutory exception to the rules governing surplus agricultural land.
material_facts: Agricultural land was gifted to persons unrelated to the donors, for natural love and affection, before the statutory cutoff date.
The revenue authorities treated the gifted land as not protected by the statutory exception when calculating surplus area, and the High Court upheld that treatment.
issues.conclusion: The gifts were not transfers for consideration within the statutory exception and were properly excluded from its protection; the appeals were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 122 of the Transfer of Property Act, a gift is made voluntarily and without consideration. The term “consideration” in that Act bears the sense given to it by section 2(d) of the Contract Act and excludes natural love and affection. Because the statutory exception in section 32FF of the PEPSU Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, protects qualifying transfers made for consideration, a gift does not fall within it. Treating such gifts as protected would defeat Chapter IV-A’s purpose of imposing land ceilings and acquiring and disposing of surplus area. James Newton v. Robert Hargreaves was distinguished because it concerned a conveyance by a father to his sons, for which natural love and affection was treated as good consideration.

predicates.surplus_land_ceiling_case: The dispute concerned whether a transfer affected the calculation or treatment of surplus agricultural land under a land-ceiling scheme.
predicates.transfer_was_gift: A landowner voluntarily transferred land to another without consideration.

issues.definition: When a dispute under a land-ceiling scheme concerns a land transfer and that transfer was a gift, the gift is not covered by an exception that requires a transfer for consideration.
